decision: How a regular's usual loaf is remembered and prefilled
options: Remember this device with a one-tap usual
Ask for phone number once, look up usual
No memory, pick each time
recommendation: Remember this device with a one-tap usual
reason: A simple device cookie plus stored last order gives a one-tap reorder without accounts or passwords.

decision: How a regular's usual loaf is remembered and prefilled
What happens when the last sourdough is taken by two people at once
options: First confirmed order wins, other sees sold-out and alternatives
Allow oversell and let bakery sort it out
Hold items in cart for a few minutes
recommendation: First confirmed order wins, other sees sold-out and alternatives
reason: An atomic stock check at confirmation is the plain, proven way to never promise a loaf that is gone.

decision: Whether customers pay online or at pickup
options: Pay at pickup, order is held
Pay online by card
Either, customer chooses
recommendation: Pay at pickup, order is held
reason: Skipping payment processing keeps the build small and fee-free, matching a neighborhood bakery.
question: What would make a regular feel their loaf is truly theirs before they arrive?

decision: How the customer is confirmed and what happens if sending fails

Show on page only
Email only
recommendation: Show confirmation on page and send text or email, retry once
reason: The on-page confirmation is the source of truth, so a failed message never leaves the customer unsure.

Standard browse-and-pick flow only

decision: Whether regulars pay online or at pickup

Pay online up front

note: Listed the four main decisions for the bakery pre-order site, with what we'd learn first from regulars; only the weekly-buyer decision rests on the one finding.

decision: Whether customers pay online when ordering or at the counter on pickup
options: Pay at the counter on pickup
Pay online when ordering
Let the customer choose either
recommendation: Pay at the counter on pickup
reason: Regulars already pay at the shop, so holding their usual with no card step keeps it effortless and the site avoids processing fees.
question: What would a regular expect to do about paying when the baker already knows them?

decision: What happens to a held loaf that is not collected
options: Hold until a set time, then release it to others
Hold all day, no release
Release it and ask for a deposit next time
recommendation: Hold until a set time, then release it to others
reason: Uncollected sourdough is the bakery's main money risk, and a clear cutoff protects it without charging regulars.
question: When a regular does not turn up for their loaf, what should the baker do?

decision: Whether a deposit is taken to hold limited loaves like the sourdough
options: No deposit for anyone
Deposit only on large or special orders
Deposit on every order
recommendation: No deposit for anyone
reason: A deposit adds friction for trusted regulars, and a small bakery can start by seeing how many loaves go uncollected.

decision: How prices are shown and set on the site
options: Same shelf prices as in the shop, no fees
Small pre-order premium
Pre-order discount for regulars
recommendation: Same shelf prices as in the shop, no fees
reason: Matching the shop keeps trust and means the site costs customers nothing extra, so the baker owns the price.

note: Pricing and payment decisions for the bakery pre-order site, built around morning regulars getting their usual loaf held.

decision: Whether a regular's usual loaf is held automatically each morning
options: Count held-usual orders per regular per week, keep usual loaf and pickup time
Count only one-off pre-orders, keep nothing between visits
Count held-usual orders, keep full order history
recommendation: Count held-usual orders per regular per week, keep usual loaf and pickup time
reason: This is the one number that shows regulars stopped finding their sourdough gone, and it needs only the usual loaf and time to prefill.
question: What makes a regular feel the baker really knows them when they walk in each morning?

label: Hold your usual
reason: This is the one number that shows regulars stopped finding their sourdough gone, and it needs only the usual loaf and time to prefill.

What single number says the site worked overall
options: Share of regulars' weekday visits that were pre-ordered
Total online orders per week
Count of sourdough sellouts before nine
recommendation: Share of regulars' weekday visits that were pre-ordered
reason: It shows whether the target regulars have actually made ordering ahead their habit, not just whether orders happen.
question: What would tell you a morning regular is truly better off because of this site?

decision: How to tell a returning regular from a new visitor at browsing
options: Count returning-visitor sessions that reach order in one tap, keep a remembered-customer token
Ask everyone to create an account, count sign-ups
Count anonymous sessions only, keep nothing
recommendation: Count returning-visitor sessions that reach order in one tap, keep a remembered-customer token
reason: It lets us measure whether we avoid asking what we already know without forcing an account on regulars.

decision: What to keep and for how long from pickup and collection
options: Count orders collected versus not collected, keep name and phone 90 days
Count collections, keep contact details indefinitely
Do not track collection at all
recommendation: Count orders collected versus not collected, keep name and phone 90 days
reason: No-shows tell the bakery if holding loaves wastes bread, and a short retention limits personal data kept.

note: Walked the journey box by box and picked the single measure and kept field per step that a decision would use.

decision: What ordering should feel like for a regular: one-tap remembered usual, or a guided browse-and-pick flow
options: Remembered: usual loaf prefilled, one tap to hold it
Guided: browse, pick, time, pay in steps
Remembered for regulars, guided for newcomers
recommendation: Remembered for regulars, guided for newcomers
reason: The grey wireframes hinge on this: one filled button marks the main action, and regulars should never be asked what the bakery already knows.
question: What would make a regular feel the baker already knows them the moment they open the page?

decision: What leads the first screen: the regular's usual loaf held, or the full bread menu
options: Usual loaf and pickup time first, menu below
Full bread menu first, usual as a shortcut
Menu only, no usual on the first screen
recommendation: Usual loaf and pickup time first, menu below
reason: Hierarchy follows the main job: the usual sits at the top with one filled button, and the menu is quiet secondary content.
question: When a regular arrives at nine and the sourdough is nearly gone, what do they most want to see first?

label: Hold your usual
reason: Hierarchy follows the main job: the usual sits at the top with one filled button, and the menu is quiet secondary content.
decision: What leads the first screen: the regular's usual loaf held, or the full bread menu
What a sold-out or nearly-gone loaf shows on screen
options: Greyed out with the next available day and a hold option
Hidden from the list until it is back
Shown with a plain count of loaves left
recommendation: Greyed out with the next available day and a hold option
reason: The empty state must say what happens next in plain words, since sourdough selling out early is the exact pain regulars feel.

decision: Which single accent colour and type pairing gives the page a warm neighbourhood-bakery feel
options: Warm crust-brown accent on cream paper, one serif display with a sans text face
Deep green accent on off-white, sans only
Tomato red accent on white, rounded display
recommendation: Warm crust-brown accent on cream paper, one serif display with a sans text face
reason: Interface stays 90 to 95% neutral with one accent and two type faces with fixed jobs, and crust-brown reads familiar, not violet or loud.

note: Sketched the regular's flow in grey: what the whole ordering feels like, what leads the first screen, how sold-out looks, and the single accent.

decision: Who the first version is built for
options: Morning regulars only
Regulars first, occasional buyers can also order
Everyone equally
recommendation: Morning regulars only
reason: Regulars have the clearest pain (usual sourdough gone by nine), so building for them first keeps the version small and testable.
question: What is it about the morning rush that makes a regular feel let down when their loaf is gone?

decision: How a regular's usual loaf gets held
options: One tap to hold usual, prefilled and remembered
Regular picks loaves each time from the full menu
Standing daily order that repeats automatically
recommendation: One tap to hold usual, prefilled and remembered
reason: It delivers the feeling of being known and never asks for what the bakery already knows.
question: How should it feel when the baker already knows what you want before you ask?

label: Hold your usual
reason: It delivers the feeling of being known and never asks for what the bakery already knows.
decision: How a regular's usual loaf gets held
What happens when the usual loaf is sold out or the hold is missed
options: Show sold out early and offer a close alternative; release held loaves after a grace time
Hold loaves all day with no release
Let the baker decide each case by hand
recommendation: Show sold out early and offer a close alternative; release held loaves after a grace time
reason: Sourdough sells out early, so the promise only works if holds are honest and unclaimed loaves go back on sale.
question: When a regular's usual is gone or left uncollected, what would feel fair to them and to the baker?
